narrative:
The model estimated a 59.6% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. In practical terms, it judged failure more likely than passing, and that risk estimate led to the denial of your law school application.

The strongest factor increasing that risk was your undergraduate GPA. At 3.30, it is slightly above the 3.23 average among accepted students, so this is not a simple “low GPA” rejection; in your full profile, it was still the largest warning signal. The second most influential factor was your third-year class standing. Your third-year decile of 9 is much stronger than the accepted-student average of 5.79, and this factor pushed the prediction toward passing, making it the main point in your favor. The third factor was your LSAT score. Your score of 40 is above the accepted-student average of 37.18, but it added a modest amount of risk in context.

Next, ask admissions for an individualized human review and an explanation of how this prediction was used. Provide context that may not be captured, such as grade trends, work or caregiving responsibilities, and a concrete bar-prep plan; ask whether a higher LSAT retake or additional academic references could support reconsideration. Also speak with a pre-law advisor about strengthening your application before reapplying.
